newsitem.title: CROATIA: Croatia orders crackdown on privatisation fraud.
newsitem.headline: Croatia orders crackdown on privatisation fraud.

text.p: The Croatian government, whose popularity has been declining over corruption allegations, has ordered a crackdown on fraud in the sale of state firms.

The move was announced on Thursday night after a session of the Defence and National Security Council chaired by President Franjo Tudjman, apparently concerned about the image of his ruling nationalist HDZ party.
The council ordered concrete steps taken against "criminal acts and malpractices in economy...in particular, abuses in the process of privatisation".
A council statement said all executive and judiciary bodies were to take "accelerated action" against corruption and all officials implicated in fraud should be sacked.
The HDZ's majority in parliament was slashed to a minimum in a general election a year ago marked by a voter backlash against perceived nationalist corruption and arrogance in power.
Analysts say the HDZ will be hardpressed to preserve its domination of municipal governments in communal elections in 1997. A presidential election is to be held by August 1997.

The Council of Europe, antechamber of the European Union, admitted Croatia as its 40th member state last week. The Zagreb government is keen to show it is building a legitimate free market economy to qualify for EU aid and closer links.
The anti-fraud drive was unveiled only two days after Tudjman told journalists his government had allowed no one to get rich illegally from privatisation.

The few Croatian newspapers not under HDZ control have been publishing accounts of privatisation fraud since Tudjman's nationalist movement ousted communists from power in 1990 elections and led Croatia to independence from Yugoslavia.
Independent journalists regularly report lucrative state properties being bought for pittances, nepotism and other irregularities by Croats exploiting high-level government connections.

A conspicuous nouveau-riche elite has emerged while much of the pre-independence middle class was reduced to near-poverty by hyper-inflation and profiteering prevalent during the 1991-95 ethnic wars in the region of former Yugoslavia.
Tudjman said in his televised interview that stories of the Croatian economy being ruled "by a dozen billionaires, speculators, war profiteers and marauders" were unfounded.
Centre-left political rivals rejected Tudjman's assessment.
